items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5136

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law and the public health law, in
relation to pharmacy services provided by managed care providers and to
repeal sections 1 and 1-a of part FFF of chapter 56 of the laws of 2020
relating to directing the department of health to remove the pharmacy
benefit from the managed care benefit package and to provide the pharma-
cy benefit under the fee for service program, in relation thereto

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to repeal the transition of the Medicaid
pharmacy benefit from managed care to fee-for-service, which would cause
unintentional harm to certain providers participating in the federal
340B program, while still maintaining protections for pharmacy oper-
ations and reducing administrative costs associated with the 340B
program.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill would repeal Sections 1 and 1-a of part FFF of
chapter 56 of the laws of 2020 that authorizes the Department of Health
(DOH) to transition the pharmacy benefit from managed care into fee-for-
service.

Section 2 of the bill requires all managed care providers and pharmacy
benefit managers to use the feefor-service preferred drug list in devel-
oping their formulary. All managed care organizations and pharmacy bene-
fit managers would be required to reimburse retail pharmacies and 340B
covered entity providers for each drug at the National Average Drug
Acquisition Cost (NADAC) plus a tiered volume-based dispensing fee to be
determined by DOH. If a specific drug does not have a NADAC rate, then
feefor-service reimbursement methodologies would be used. The bill
requires the dispensing fee set by the Commissioner of DOH to be an
amount of at least $8.50, but would allow for it to be increased above
this amount for smaller pharmacies dispensing lower volumes that may be
subject to higher operational costs. Managed care providers would be
prohibited from denying retail pharmacies the opportunity to participate
in their network under Medicaid under certain conditions. Contract phar-
macies performing services under the 340B program would be reimbursed
under a fee schedule that is based on fair market principles and cannot
be a percentage of a claim's total reimbursement or net margin.

Section 3 would prohibit pharmacy benefit managers from limiting an
individual's choice to receive their medication form their local, non-
mail order pharmacy of choice.

Section 4 is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The SFY 2020-21 final adopted budget included a provision that transi-
tions the Medicaid pharmacy benefit from managed care to the fee-for-
service program. While the implementation of the transition was delayed
for two years in the SFY 2021-22 budget, the transition is now set to go
forward on April 1, 2023.  The transition eliminates the ability of
safety-net providers to utilize savings from the federal 340B program,
as that program can only operate under managed care and not fee-for-ser-
vice. The 340B drug rebate program provides funding to safety-net
providers that is used to expand healthcare services and other programs
for vulnerable, high-need populations. Some estimates show that safety-
net providers will lose hundreds of millions of dollars from lost 340B
funding.

This bill maintains the pharmacy benefit within managed care, which
preserves the 340B drug rebate mechanism. Instead, a single Preferred
Drug List (PDL) would be created that would require uniform utilization
review management protocols, enhance the State's negotiating power for
drug rebates, and provide greater transparency in the program. The bill
will also end restrictive and anti-competitive pharmacy benefit manager
(PBM) practices by protecting pharmacy networks, limiting fees that
PBM's and other third-party middlemen siphon from the program, and phar-
macists will receive a fair and transparent dispensing fee.

This bill achieves many of the same goals of the original carveout, but
with much less disruption to important safety-net providers across the
state.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Undetermined, but potential savings to the Medicaid program from effi-
ciencies in the single formulary.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately; except that sections two and
three shall take effect April 1, 2023.

summary: Relates to pharmacy services provided by managed care providers; requires pharmacy benefit managers and managed care providers to reimburse retail pharmacies for each outpatient drug, at the National Average Drug Acquisition Cost (NADAC); repeals related provisions.
